claim: Estrogen Receptor-alpha (ER) drives 75% of breast cancers.
source: Estrogen Receptor-alpha (ER) drives 75% of breast cancers.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract presenting established knowledge about ER's role in breast cancer.

claim: Stimulation of the ER by estra-2-diol forms a transcriptionally-active chromatin-bound complex.
source: Stimulation of the ER by estra-2-diol forms a transcriptionally-active chromatin-bound complex.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about ER activation mechanism.

claim: Previous studies reported that ER binding follows a cyclical pattern.
source: Previous studies reported that ER binding follows a cyclical pattern.
evidence: This claim references prior literature findings, supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Most studies on ER cycling have been limited to individual ER target genes and without replicates.
source: However, most studies have been limited to individual ER target genes and without replicates.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the literature discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The robustness and generality of ER cycling are not well understood.
source: Thus, the robustness and generality of ER cycling are not well understood.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the limitations of previous studies.

claim: The study presents a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of the ER after activation, based on 6 replicates at 10 time-points.
source: We present a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of the ER after activation, based on 6 replicates at 10 time-points, using our method for precise quantification of binding, Parallel-Factor ChIP-seq.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: The study used Parallel-Factor ChIP-seq method for precise quantification of binding.
source: We present a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of the ER after activation, based on 6 replicates at 10 time-points, using our method for precise quantification of binding, Parallel-Factor ChIP-seq.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study identified a sustained increase in ER affinity after activation.
source: In contrast to previous studies, we identified a sustained increase in affinity, alongside a class of estra-2-diol independent binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented.

claim: The study identified a class of estra-2-diol independent ER binding sites.
source: In contrast to previous studies, we identified a sustained increase in affinity, alongside a class of estra-2-diol independent binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented.

claim: The results are corroborated by quantitative re-analysis of multiple independent studies.
source: Our results are corroborated by quantitative re-analysis of multiple independent studies.
evidence: This refers to additional analysis performed on published data.

claim: The new model reconciles conflicting studies into the ER at the TFF1 promoter.
source: Our new model reconciles the conflicting studies into the ER at the TFF1 promoter and provides a detailed understanding in the context of the ER's role as both the driver and therapeutic target of breast cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration of current and previous findings.

claim: The ER is one of a family of transcription factors called nuclear receptors.
source: The ER is one of a family of transcription factors called nuclear receptors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ER classification.

claim: Nuclear receptors are intra-cellular and, on activation by their ligand, typically undergo dimerisation and bind to specific DNA motif.
source: Nuclear receptors are intra-cellular and, on activation by their ligand, typically undergo dimerisation and bind to specific DNA motif (for ER: Estrogen Response Elements; EREs).
evidence: This describes the general mechanism of nuclear receptor function based on established knowledge.

claim: ER binds to Estrogen Response Elements (EREs).
source: Nuclear receptors are intra-cellular and, on activation by their ligand, typically undergo dimerisation and bind to specific DNA motif (for ER: Estrogen Response Elements; EREs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ER-DNA binding specificity.

claim: On the chromatin, the nuclear receptor recruits a series of cofactors and promotes the basal transcription mechanism at either nearby promoters or through chromatin loops from distal enhancers.
source: On the chromatin, the nuclear receptor recruits a series of cofactors and promotes the basal transcription mechanism at either nearby promoters or through chromatin loops from distal enhancers.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of nuclear receptor-mediated transcription.

claim: Nuclear receptors have become a model system for transcription factor analysis due to their minimal nature relative to other signaling pathways.
source: Because of the minimal nature of these systems relative to other signaling pathways, nuclear receptors have become a model system for transcription factor analysis.
evidence: This is an inference about why nuclear receptors are studied, based on their characteristics.

claim: Nuclear receptors play a role as drivers in a range of hormone dependent cancers.
source: Simultaneously, the role of nuclear receptors as drivers in a range of hormone dependent cancers has led to focused studies in the context of the disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear receptors in cancer biology.

claim: The ER and key cofactors followed a cyclical pattern in breast cancer cell lines with maximal binding at 45 min after stimulation with estra-2-diol, as reported by Shang et al., 2000.
source: Previously, it was reported that the ER and key cofactors followed a cyclical pattern in breast cancer cell lines with maximal binding at 45 min after stimulation with estra-2-diol (Shang et al., 2000; Métivier et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Similar cyclical results were reported for the AR after activation with DHT by Kang et al., 2002.
source: Similar results were also reported for the AR after activation with DHT (Kang et al., 2002) and several follow-up studies exist looking at single genomic loci (Herynk et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2005; Shao et al., 2004; Burakov et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Several follow-up studies exist looking at single genomic loci for nuclear receptor cycling.
source: Similar results were also reported for the AR after activation with DHT (Kang et al., 2002) and several follow-up studies exist looking at single genomic loci (Herynk et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2005; Shao et al., 2004; Burakov et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Subsequent genome-wide studies have provided little further detail on the specific nature of the proposed kinetics of ER binding.
source: However, subsequent genome-wide studies have provided little further detail on the specific nature of the proposed kinetics of ER binding being either limited in the number of replicates or lacking temporal resolution (Honkela et al., 2015; wa Maina et al., 2014; Dzida et al., 2017; Guertin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on review of cited genome-wide studies.

claim: In the authors' own network analysis (Holding et al., 2018), they focused on 0, 45 and 90 min and found no significant reduction in ER signal at 90 min.
source: In our own network analysis (Holding et al., 2018), we focused on 0, 45 and 90 min and found no significant reduction in ER signal at 90 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Quantitative proteomic analysis of ER interactions at 0, 45, and 90 min by qPLEX-RIME shows no significant difference in terms of ER interactions at 45 and 90 min.
source: In the same study, quantitative proteomic analysis of ER interactions at the same time intervals by qPLEX-RIME (Papachristou et al., 2018) shows no significant difference in terms of ER interactions at 45 and 90 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The conflicting results about ER cycling have not been resolved.
source: These conflicting results have so far not been resolved.
evidence: This is an inference about the state of the field based on the literature review.

claim: Routinely used assays to measure protein binding to chromatin are based on Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP).
source: Routinely used assays to measure protein binding to chromatin are based on Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ChIP methodology.

claim: A major challenge to monitoring ER activation through ChIP is the normalization of the ChIP signal.
source: A major challenge to monitoring ER activation through ChIP is the normalization of the ChIP signal — either genome-wide with next generation sequencing or at individual loci by qPCR — as the standard protocols do not control for a significant number of confounding factors including the efficiency of the immunoprecipitation step.
evidence: This is an inference about technical challenges based on knowledge of ChIP methodology.

claim: Standard ChIP protocols do not control for a significant number of confounding factors including the efficiency of the immunoprecipitation step.
source: A major challenge to monitoring ER activation through ChIP is the normalization of the ChIP signal — either genome-wide with next generation sequencing or at individual loci by qPCR — as the standard protocols do not control for a significant number of confounding factors including the efficiency of the immunoprecipitation step.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of ChIP methodology limitations.

claim: The two original ER cycling studies (Shang et al., 2000; Métivier et al., 2003) provided only limited controls for normalization.
source: In the case the of the two original studies (Shang et al., 2000; Métivier et al., 2003), the data only provided limited controls in this regard.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the cited studies.

claim: An alternative method to normalize ChIP-seq data is to use the maximal read count obtained at each individual site across each time point, as applied by Guertin et al., 2014.
source: An alternative method that has been applied to normalize ChIP-seq data is to use the maximal read count obtained at each individual site across each time point (Guertin et al., 2014); however, this method is at the expense of monitoring the magnitude of ER binding and gives equal weight to low read count peaks and more robust data from stronger binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Normalizing ChIP-seq data by maximal read count is at the expense of monitoring the magnitude of ER binding and gives equal weight to low read count peaks and more robust data from stronger binding sites.
source: An alternative method that has been applied to normalize ChIP-seq data is to use the maximal read count obtained at each individual site across each time point (Guertin et al., 2014); however, this method is at the expense of monitoring the magnitude of ER binding and gives equal weight to low read count peaks and more robust data from stronger binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the normalization method.

claim: The study generated sample data for six independent isogenic experiments to enable better characterization of the variance within the data.
source: The first strategy was to increase the number of replicates. We generated sample data for six independent isogenic experiments to enable better characterization of the variance within the data.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: The study provides twice the level of replication used in previous ChIP-qPCR studies (Métivier et al., 2003).
source: This strategy provided an unprecedented level of information regarding ER activation with twice the level of replication used in previous ChIP-qPCR studies (Métivier et al., 2003) and a significant improvement on previous single replicate genome-wide studies.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study design to previous studies.

claim: The study represents a significant improvement on previous single replicate genome-wide studies.
source: This strategy provided an unprecedented level of information regarding ER activation with twice the level of replication used in previous ChIP-qPCR studies (Métivier et al., 2003) and a significant improvement on previous single replicate genome-wide studies.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study design to previous studies.

claim: The study used Parallel-Factor ChIP (pfChIP), a recently developed method for precise quantification of binding, which uses an internal control for quantitative differential ChIP-seq.
source: The second strategy was to use our recently developed method for precise quantification of binding, Parallel-Factor ChIP (pfChIP) (Guertin et al., 2018), which uses an internal control for quantitative differential ChIP-seq.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: The combination of six replicates and pfChIP enabled the most comprehensive and precise analysis of ER activation to date.
source: Combined, these two strategies enabled us to undertake the most comprehensive and precise analysis of ER activation to date.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the current study based on its design.

claim: ER-binding was measured in MCF7 cells, a widely used model system for ER biology.
source: We measured ER-binding in MCF7 cells, a widely used model system for ER biology.
evidence: This describes the experimental system used in the study.

claim: MCF7 cells were grown from ATCC stocks, keeping passaging to a minimum.
source: To maximize the reproducibility of our results, MCF7 cells were grown from ATCC stocks, keeping passaging to a minimum, and the cell line origin was confirmed by STR genotyping.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedures used in the study.

claim: The cell line origin was confirmed by STR genotyping.
source: To maximize the reproducibility of our results, MCF7 cells were grown from ATCC stocks, keeping passaging to a minimum, and the cell line origin was confirmed by STR genotyping.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedures used in the study.

claim: CellStrainer was applied to the input data from ChIP-seq experiments to ensure the MCF7 cell line did not show significant genetic drift.
source: Additionally, to ensure the MCF7 cell line did not show significant genetic drift during culturing within our laboratory, we applied CellStrainer (Ben-David et al., 2018) to the input data from our ChIP-seq experiments.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedures used in the study.

claim: The fraction of genome with copy-number discordance was estimated at 0.2787.
source: The fraction of genome with copy-number discordance was estimated at 0.2787, within the range of 0 to 0.3 as published by CellStrainer's developers to ensure similar therapeutic response.
evidence: This is a result from the CellStrainer analysis.

claim: A copy-number discordance of 0.2787 is within the range of 0 to 0.3 as published by CellStrainer's developers to ensure similar therapeutic response.
source: The fraction of genome with copy-number discordance was estimated at 0.2787, within the range of 0 to 0.3 as published by CellStrainer's developers to ensure similar therapeutic response.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to CellStrainer's published criteria.

claim: Sequencing reads from 60 pfChip-seq samples targeting ER and six input samples were demultiplexed and aligned to the Homo sapiens GRCh38 reference assembly.
source: Sequencing reads from the analysis of 60 pfChip-seq samples targeting ER and six input samples were demultiplexed and aligned to the Homo sapiens GRCh38 reference assembly.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedures used in the study.

claim: Visual inspection of the data using IGV Viewer confirmed enrichment at known ER binding sites.
source: Visual inspection of the data using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) Viewer (Robinson et al., 2011) confirmed enrichment at known ER binding sites (exemplified by TFF1 in Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and the presence of previously reported CTCF control peaks (Guertin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the data, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Visual inspection confirmed the presence of previously reported CTCF control peaks.
source: Visual inspection of the data using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) Viewer (Robinson et al., 2011) confirmed enrichment at known ER binding sites (exemplified by TFF1 in Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and the presence of previously reported CTCF control peaks (Guertin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the data, supported by citation.

claim: pfChIP-seq samples qualitatively showed minimal ER binding at 0 min.
source: From visual inspection, pfChIP-seq samples qualitatively showed minimal ER binding at 0 min while CTCF binding was constant at all time points.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the data.

claim: CTCF binding was constant at all time points.
source: From visual inspection, pfChIP-seq samples qualitatively showed minimal ER binding at 0 min while CTCF binding was constant at all time points.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the data.

claim: Peak count data from CTCF binding sites were used to normalize between conditions as these sites have previously been shown to be unchanged in response to estrogen.
source: Peak count data from CTCF binding sites were used to normalize between conditions as these sites have previously been shown to be unchanged in response to estrogen (Ross-Innes et al., 2011), with >70 000 binding sites discovered across all samples and >50 000 CTCF binding sites found in over 50% of samples.
evidence: This describes the normalization strategy, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: More than 70,000 CTCF binding sites were discovered across all samples.
source: Peak count data from CTCF binding sites were used to normalize between conditions as these sites have previously been shown to be unchanged in response to estrogen (Ross-Innes et al., 2011), with >70 000 binding sites discovered across all samples and >50 000 CTCF binding sites found in over 50% of samples.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: More than 50,000 CTCF binding sites were found in over 50% of samples.
source: Peak count data from CTCF binding sites were used to normalize between conditions as these sites have previously been shown to be unchanged in response to estrogen (Ross-Innes et al., 2011), with >70 000 binding sites discovered across all samples and >50 000 CTCF binding sites found in over 50% of samples.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Analysis after normalization of the raw data showed similar levels of variability in terms of signal as seen when developing the pfChIP method.
source: Analysis after normalization of the raw data showed similar levels of variability in terms of signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) as we saw when developing the pfChIP method (Guertin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current data to previous work, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: The normalized binding matrix of ER binding was used for all downstream analyses.
source: The resultant normalized binding matrix of ER binding was used for all downstream analyses and is provided as Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This describes the data processing workflow.

claim: On activation with estra-2-diol, the ER rapidly (in less than 10 min) binds the TFF1 promoter.
source: Normalized count data for the TFF1 promoter showed that on activation with estra-2-diol the ER rapidly (in less than 10 min) binds the TFF1 promoter.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: ER binding at the TFF1 promoter after 10 min shows no significant changes.
source: Binding after this time point shows no significant changes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Analysis of the data by individual replicates did not demonstrate evidence of oscillatory binding in individual replicates either with a period of 90 min or an alternative frequency.
source: Analysis of the data by individual replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) did not demonstrate evidence of oscillatory binding in individual replicates either with a period of 90 min period or an alternative frequency.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: There is significantly more variance in ER binding after induction than in CTCF binding between replicates.
source: Comparison of the variance in the ER binding after induction shows that there is significantly more variance (F-test, time points >= 10 min, p-value < 1 × 10-10) in the ER binding data than in CTCF binding between replicates.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Pairwise F-test for ER binding at all time points showed no significant difference in the variance for any comparison.
source: In contrast, pairwise F-test (two-sided, FDR < 0.05) for ER binding at all time points showed no significant difference in the variance for any comparison.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The variance of CTCF binding in pfChIP-seq is a good estimator of the technical variance.
source: As the variance of CTCF binding in pfChIP-seq is a good estimator of the technical variance, the most likely source of increased variance in ER binding is therefore biological.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the pfChIP-seq method.

claim: The most likely source of increased variance in ER binding is biological.
source: As the variance of CTCF binding in pfChIP-seq is a good estimator of the technical variance, the most likely source of increased variance in ER binding is therefore biological.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ER and CTCF variance.

claim: Findings at the TFF1 promoter were validated through analysis of the RARA promoter and proximal CTCF peaks.
source: These findings were validated through analysis of the RARA promoter and proximal CTCF peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), which gave consistent results to those seen at the TFF1 promoter.
evidence: This describes validation of the findings using additional genomic loci.

claim: ER binding sites were shown to reach maximum occupancy at different time points depending on genomic location, revealing a P300 squelching mechanism at early time points, as reported by Guertin et al., 2014.
source: Previously, ER binding sites were shown to reach maximum occupancy at different time points depending on genomic location, revealing a P300 squelching mechanism at early time points (Guertin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The two time points with the largest numbers of sites reaching maximal occupancy in both the current and Guertin et al.'s data sets were at 10 and 40 min.
source: Consistent with the previous study, the two time points with the largest numbers of sites reaching maximal occupancy in both data sets were at 10 and 40 min (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis comparing current and previous studies.

claim: Grouping by maximum occupancy distorts the data and the effects that drove the appearance of blocks are not statistically significant in the current dataset with the exception of the 0 to 10 min contrast.
source: While grouping by maximum occupancy in Figure 2A was essential to highlight these features in the context of Guertin et al.'s previous study, in our analysis we found this method distorts the data and the effects that drove the appearance of blocks are not statistically significant in our dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with the exception of the 0 to 10 min contrast.
evidence: This is an inference about the normalization method based on statistical analysis.

claim: The loss of ER binding on activation with estra-2-diol is unprecedented.
source: As far as we are aware, the loss on ER binding on activation with estra-2-diol is unprecedented, and therefore the presence of a block of ER sites with maximal binding at 0 min warranted deeper investigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the literature.

claim: Analysis of the class average for sites with maximal binding at 0 min showed that the variance of this class is much greater than the decrease seen between 0 and 10 min.
source: Analysis of the class average (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) showed that the variance of this class is much greater than the decrease seen between 0 and 10 min.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Analysis of individual trajectories of each binding site with maximal binding at 0 min showed the maximal binding at time zero appearing marginal in all cases.
source: A more detailed analysis of the individual trajectories of each binding site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) showed a similar result, with the maximal binding at time zero appearing marginal and in all cases.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: pfChIP-seq allowed direct normalization of the data to the internal control, providing quantification of the absolute binding affinity at each time point.
source: pfChIP-seq allowed us to improve on the previous study by directly normalizing the data to the internal control. The resultant binding matrix provided quantification of the absolute binding affinity at each time point (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the advantage of the pfChIP-seq method.

claim: Relative normalization to maximum binding emphasizes binding maxima while absolute normalization to an internal control shows that these maxima are very shallow.
source: Comparison of Figure 2A and B demonstrates the effects of different data normalization strategies. The relative normalization to maximum binding emphasizes binding maxima (red blocks in Figure 2A) while the absolute normalization to an internal control shows that these maxima are very shallow, barely visible in Figure 2B, and other features dominate the data.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of normalization strategies based on comparison of figures.

claim: A few genes show very high levels of ER binding, while most genes show intermediate levels and some very low levels, with only time point 0 showing very low levels for all genes.
source: A few genes show very high levels of ER binding (visible as thin red lines in Figure 2B), while most genes show intermediate levels and some very low levels (blue lines). These different levels of ER binding are preserved over time, with only time point 0 showing very low levels for all genes.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: t-SNE analysis revealed two major trajectories of binding sites in the data, one dominated by low FDR and one by high FDR.
source: To elucidate potential different temporal responses to ER activation by estra-2-diol, we applied t-SNE (Maaten and Hinton, 2008), a widely used method for dimensionality reduction and data visualization (Figure 3). Each dot in the plot represents a binding site over time, that is one row in the binding matrix shown in Figure 2B. We colored each dot by the false discovery rate (FDR; (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995)) for the change in ER affinity between 0 to 10 min. This analysis revealed two major trajectories of binding sites in the data, one dominated by low FDR (orange) and one by high FDR (blue).
evidence: This is a result from the t-SNE analysis.

claim: Both trajectories saw an increasing affinity in the direction of the white arrow.
source: Both trajectories saw an increasing affinity in the direction of the white arrow.
evidence: This is a result from the t-SNE analysis.

claim: The pattern of two trajectories was stable for a wide range of perplexity, the main t-SNE parameter.
source: This pattern was stable for a wide range of perplexity, the main t-SNE parameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the robustness of the t-SNE analysis.

claim: Trajectory A demonstrates increasing ER affinity in response to estra-2-diol at 10 min.
source: We named the estra-2-diol responsive trajectory A, and the estra-2-diol independent trajectory B.
evidence: This is a characterization of the trajectories based on the data analysis.

claim: Trajectory B shows increasing affinity for all time points, that is estra-2-diol independent binding, but the maximum signal is of a lower intensity than that of Trajectory A.
source: We named the estra-2-diol responsive trajectory A, and the estra-2-diol independent trajectory B.
evidence: This is a characterization of the trajectories based on the data analysis.

claim: De novo motif analysis for Class A gave strongest enrichment for the ERE (p = 1 × 10-538).
source: De novo motif analysis for Class A (the peaks found at the end of trajectory A) gave strongest enrichment for the ERE (p = 1 × 10-538).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis.

claim: Analysis of Class C provided a partial ERE, consistent with ER affinity being a function of how conserved the ER binding site is with respect to ideal ERE.
source: The same analysis of Class C provided a partial ERE (not shown), consistent with ER affinity being a function of how conserved the ER binding site is with respect to ideal ERE.
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis and an inference about the relationship between motif conservation and binding affinity.

claim: Analysis of Class B gave FOXA1 as the most significantly enriched motif (p = 1 × 10-19).
source: Analysis of Class B gave FOXA1 as the most significantly enriched motif (p = 1 × 10-19).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis.

claim: Class A showed minimal binding at 0 min followed by a robust response before 10 min, then the binding affinity remained similar for the remaining time points.
source: Average binding profiles were computed for both Class A and Class B. Class A showed minimal binding at 0 min followed by a robust response before 10 min, the binding affinity then remained similar for the remaining time points.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis of average binding profiles.

claim: Class B displayed estra-2-diol independent binding at 0 min and average ER binding affinity saw no significant changes between time points.
source: In contrast, Class B displayed estra-2-diol independent binding at 0 min and average ER binding affinity saw no significant changes between time points.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis of average binding profiles.

claim: Class C gave a similar profile to Class A, but with reduced amplitude.
source: Class C gave a similar profile to Class A (not shown), but with reduced amplitude.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis of average binding profiles.

claim: The average amplitude of the binding from 10 to 90 min displayed a greater ER affinity for Class A than Class B.
source: The average amplitude of the binding from 10 to 90 min displayed a greater ER affinity for Class A then Class B.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis comparing Class A and Class B.

claim: GREAT analysis of Class B binding sites identified the enrichment of six amplicons previously identified from the analysis of 191 breast tumor samples.
source: Genomic regions enrichment of annotations tool (GREAT) analysis (Welch et al., 2014) of Class B binding sites (Supplementary file 2) identified the enrichment of six amplicons previously identified from the analysis of 191 breast tumor samples, q = 5.6 × 10-41 to q = 3.3 × 10-8, (Nikolsky et al., 2008) and a set of genes upregulated in luminal-like breast cancer cell lines compared to the mesenchymal-like cell lines, q = 1.9 × 10-13, [Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is a result from the GREAT analysis, supported by citations.

claim: GREAT analysis of Class B binding sites identified a set of genes upregulated in luminal-like breast cancer cell lines compared to the mesenchymal-like cell lines.
source: Genomic regions enrichment of annotations tool (GREAT) analysis (Welch et al., 2014) of Class B binding sites (Supplementary file 2) identified the enrichment of six amplicons previously identified from the analysis of 191 breast tumor samples, q = 5.6 × 10-41 to q = 3.3 × 10-8, (Nikolsky et al., 2008) and a set of genes upregulated in luminal-like breast cancer cell lines compared to the mesenchymal-like cell lines, q = 1.9 × 10-13, [Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is a result from the GREAT analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Analysis of the ER only ChIP-seq data stream gave very similar results to that of pfChIP-seq analysis, confirming that any potential cycling is not suppressed by the method.
source: Undertaking the same analysis of the ER only ChIP-seq data stream gave very similar results to that of pfChIP-seq analysis, confirming that any potential cycling is not suppressed by the method (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis to validate the pfChIP-seq method.

claim: No clear cycling was seen for the individual replicates in the ER only ChIP-seq analysis.
source: As with the pfChIP-seq analysis, no clear cycling was seen for the individual replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Class A binding sites showed the strongest response to estra-2-diol, the greatest enrichment of the estrogen response element and contained the classical ER binding site at TFF1.
source: Class A binding sites showed the strongest response to estra-2-diol, the greatest enrichment of the estrogen response element and contained the classical ER binding site at TFF1.
evidence: This is a summary of the characteristics of Class A sites based on the data analysis.

claim: A t-SNE plot of only Class A sites did not provide distinct clustering of points.
source: A t-SNE plot of only Class A sites (Figure 4A) did not provide distinct clustering of points.
evidence: This is a result from the t-SNE analysis of Class A sites.

claim: Partial separation in the t-SNE plot of Class A sites was seen on the basis of time point of maximal binding (left to right) and amplitude (approximately top to bottom).
source: Partial separation was seen on the basis of time point of maximal binding (left to right) and amplitude (approximately top to bottom).
evidence: This is a result from the t-SNE analysis of Class A sites.

claim: Profiles for binding sites near the transcription start site of TFF1 and GREB1 gave a robust sustained response to estra-2-diol.
source: Profiles for binding sites near the transcription start site of two well studied ER target genes, TFF1 and GREB1, gave a robust sustained response to estra-2-diol.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of individual binding sites.

claim: ER binding at TFF1 was stable after induction.
source: As previously seen in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, ER binding at TFF1 was stable after induction.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Analysis of ER binding proximal to GREB1 showed a robust and unidirectional response to estra-2-diol.
source: Analysis of ER binding proximal to GREB1 again showed a robust and unidirectional response to estra-2-diol.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Several studies undertook the same analysis as Shang et al., 2000 in the MCF7 cell line, with the same concentration of estra-2-diol, same crosslinking time scale, and at the same promoter.
source: By manually reviewing the first 1000 citations of (Shang et al., 2000), we identified several studies (Burakov et al., 2002; Herynk et al., 2010; Shao et al., 2004) that undertook the same analysis in the MCF7 cell line, with the same concentration of estra-2-diol, same crosslinking time scale, and at the same promoter as the best datasets for comparison with each other and to our dataset.
evidence: This describes the literature review process and selection criteria for comparison studies.

claim: Comparison of the data from four studies gave little or no consistency in the temporal profile of ER, AIB1 and P300 binding at the TFF1 promoter.
source: Comparison of the data from all four studies gave little or no consistency in the temporal profile of ER, AIB1 and P300 binding at these sites (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis of multiple studies.

claim: The primary data from the four comparison studies was not available.
source: Quantitative image analysis presents limitations in reestablishing the exact values without the primary data; however, the primary data was not available.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the comparative analysis.

claim: The comparison studies only report a single replicate for analysis, making it impossible to quantify uncertainty in the data.
source: Interpretation is further hindered as these studies only report a single replicate for analysis, thereby making it impossible to quantify uncertainty in the data.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the comparison studies.

claim: There is no consistent evidence for cycling in the studies using the same conditions as the original observation.
source: Therefore, there is no consistent evidence for cycling in the studies using the same conditions as the original observation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis.

claim: The sites at which ER binding was detected on the chromatin follow two distinct trajectories: rapid activation within 10 min followed by a stable response, or ligand independent binding.
source: By undertaking six biological replicates and incorporating an internal control with pfChIP, we have produced the most comprehensive analysis to date of ER binding over the first 90 min after stimulation with estra-2-diol. We found the sites at which we detected ER binding on the chromatin follows two distinct trajectories, either the rapid activation within 10 min followed by a stable response or ligand independent binding.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Enrichment of the FOXA1 motif in the strongest ligand-independent/Class B sites supports the hypothesis that these are a result of ER interactions at these sites.
source: Enrichment of the FOXA1 motif in the strongest ligand-independent/Class B sites supports our hypothesis: that these are as a result of ER interactions at these sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motif analysis results.

claim: The de novo motif analysis did not find the presence of the CTCF motif in Class B sites, confirming that they are not an artifact of utilizing CTCF to normalize via the pfChIP-seq method.
source: Importantly, the de novo motif analysis did not find the presence of the CTCF motif, confirming that they are not an artifact of utilizing CTCF to normalize via the pfChIP-seq method.
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis that validates the normalization approach.

claim: Class B sites represent open regions of chromatin where ER can be recruited by other transcription factors in the absence of its own ligand.
source: On the basis that no ERE was found at Class B sites and that the affinity of ER at these sites was less than at estra-2-diol response sites, we propose that these sites represent open regions of chromatin where ER can be recruited by other transcription factors in the absence of its own ligand.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Class B sites based on the data.

claim: ER interactions at Class B sites are weak and very likely transient.
source: However, these interactions are weak, and very likely transient, as the average binding affinity for Class B sites is similar in level (a normalized read count of 30–40) to the binding before activation at Class A binding sites, but greater than Class C binding sites (≈ 10 normalized reads increasing to ≈ 40 on activation).
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding affinity data.

claim: Ligand dependent activation of ER was seen robustly at Class A sites, but displayed no evidence of cyclical binding.
source: Ligand dependent activation of ER was seen robustly at Class A sites, but displayed no evidence of cyclical binding.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for Class A sites.

claim: ER activation occurs rapidly, within 10 min and binding shows no significant change after this point.
source: We propose instead that ER activation occurs rapidly, within 10 min and binding shows no significant change after this point.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: The examples of increasing or decreasing ER binding after activation at the SNX24 and ACKR3 TSS should be interpreted with caution as searching for individual outliers within a large data set will generate false positives.
source: The two examples we demonstrated — of increasing or decreasing ER binding after activation at the SNX24 and ACKR3 TSS (Figure 4A) — should be interpreted with caution as, while downstream effects are likely to modulate ER binding, searching for individual outliers results within a large data set will generate false positives.
evidence: This is a cautionary note about interpreting individual examples.

claim: The two examples of SNX24 and ACKR3 imply a secondary level of modulation does occur as previously seen, but at much lower magnitude than proposed in studies focused on ER cycling.
source: Nonetheless, the two examples imply a secondary level of modulation does occur as previously seen, but at much lower magnitude than proposed in studies focused on ER cycling.
evidence: This is an inference about secondary modulation based on the examples.

claim: It is unlikely that alternative conditions could induce tightly regulated cycling in terms of physiology.
source: It is possible that alternative conditions may be able to induce tightly regulated cycling; however, we feel this is unlikely in terms of physiology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the possibility of cycling under different conditions.

claim: The work of Metivier et al. makes use of α-amanitin, a RNA polymerase inhibitor, which has no direct interpretation within the cancer biology setting.
source: For example, the work of Metivier et al. makes use of α-amanitin, a RNA polymerase inhibitor. Within the cancer biology setting, these conditions have no direct interpretation.
evidence: This is a critique of the experimental conditions used in a previous study.

claim: The mode of action of α-amanitin is downstream of the ER and therefore is a confounding factor, not a clear method of synchronization.
source: Worse, the mode of action is downstream of the ER and therefore is a confounding factor, not a clear method of synchronization.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of using α-amanitin in ER studies.

claim: The previously described cyclical response kinetics are likely an artefact of observing a highly variable process without replicates.
source: In light of our results and the lack of consistency of published results, we propose that the previously described cyclical response kinetics are likely an artefact of observing a highly variable process without replicates.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the discrepancy between current and previous findings.

claim: With replicates, the cyclical effect is lost when averaging.
source: With replicates, the cyclical effect is lost when averaging.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of replication on the observed cycling.

claim: Even if a cyclical response existed, the results indicate that it is not regulated tightly enough to be coherently visible across multiple replicates.
source: Even if a cyclical response existed, our results indicate that it is not regulated tightly enough to be coherently visible across multiple replicates.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of any potential cycling based on the data.

claim: The variance in ER binding may better be described by heterogeneity in the cell populations before induction and by current models regarding expression noise as an indicator for greater transcription responsiveness.
source: The variance in ER binding may better be described by heterogeneity in the cell populations before induction and by current models regarding expression noise as an indicator for greater transcription responsiveness (Morgan and Marioni, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the variance in ER binding, supported by citation.

claim: The proposal provides, for the first time, a model that reconciles ChIP-seq data with the stochastic model of nuclear receptor binding as proposed and visualized by those undertaking single molecule imaging.
source: Finally, our proposal provides, for the first time, a model that reconciles ChIP-seq data with the stochastic model of nuclear receptor binding as proposed and visualized by those undertaking single model imaging.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the proposed model in reconciling different types of data.

claim: ER cycling has always been irreconcilable with single molecule imaging data.
source: In contrast, ER cycling has always been irreconcilable with these alternative forms of data (Lenstra et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a statement about the incompatibility of ER cycling with single molecule imaging, supported by citation.

claim: The possibility that the cells could have specifically lost the ability to regulate ER binding in the manner previously described has been minimized through the use of cells direct from ATCC, by confirming the cell line by STR genotype and applying the latest methods to confirm genetic similarity.
source: While we cannot discount that our cells could have specifically lost the ability to regulate ER binding in the manner previously described, we have minimized this possibility through the use of cells direct from ATCC, by confirming the cell line by STR genotype and applying the latest methods (Ben-David et al., 2018) to confirm that our cell line is genetically similar to the strains used in other labs.
evidence: This describes the quality control measures taken to ensure cell line authenticity.

claim: Through the use of stringent internal controls, the study reproducibly showed that estra-2-diol responsive ER binding is sustained and not cyclical, with the magnitude of the binding primarily defined by the conservation of the ERE at the binding site.
source: In summary, through the use of stringent internal controls, we have reproducibly shown that estra-2-diol responsive ER binding is sustained and not cyclical, with the magnitude of the binding primarily defined by the conservation of the ERE at the binding site.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion of the study.
